definition: The practice of the late medieval church of promising, in return for payments of money, the remission of punishment for sin in the afterlife. The sale of letters of indulgence, which among other things financed the building of St. Peter's Basilica, was the immediate occasion for Luther's 95 Theses.

A form of rule in the 17th and 18th centuries in which the monarch claimed to govern alone, free of the estates and of the laws. A standing army, a body of officials, a directed economy and a splendid court were its supports; Louis XIV of France is regarded as the model.

The central square of a Greek city, which served as market, meeting place and political center. In Athens the council house, courts, colonnades and altars stood on the agora; here Socrates held his conversations and laws were posted in public.

The upper city, a fortified hill in many Greek cities that served as citadel and sanctuary. From the 5th century BC the Acropolis of Athens bore the Parthenon, the Erechtheion and the Propylaea, and it is today the best-known group of buildings of antiquity.

The Arabic name for the parts of the Iberian Peninsula ruled by Muslims between 711 and 1492. Under the emirate and caliphate of Córdoba, al-Andalus experienced a flowering of agriculture, trade, scholarship and architecture in which Muslims, Jews and Christians all took part. After the collapse of the caliphate in 1031 it lost ground piece by piece to the Christian kingdoms, until with Granada the last remnant fell.

A writing system in which each sign stands for a single sound, so that every word can be written with a small number of letters. The Phoenician alphabet of 22 consonant signs arose around 1050 BC and is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic writing.

The longest section of human history, from the first stone tools around 2.6 million years ago to the end of the last Ice Age about 12,000 years ago. People lived as roaming hunters and gatherers and made tools of stone, bone and wood.

The policy of Great Britain and France in the 1930s of satisfying Hitler's demands through concessions in order to avoid another war. It culminated in the Munich Agreement of 1938 and failed when Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939. Since then the term has stood for giving way to aggressors.

A style of rule in the 18th century in which monarchs adopted ideas of the Enlightenment such as religious toleration, legal reform and schooling, without sharing their power. Frederick II of Prussia, Maria Theresa, Joseph II and Catherine II saw themselves as the first servants of their state.

An intellectual movement of the 18th century that sought to make reason, criticism and experience the foundation of knowledge, law and politics. Its representatives called for toleration, human rights, the separation of powers and education for all, and thereby prepared the way for the revolutions in America and France.

A state examination system in China by which, from the Han period onward and increasingly from the Tang, officials were selected according to their knowledge of the Confucian classics. It was intended to award offices by merit rather than by birth and shaped education in East Asia until 1905.

An association of states founded in Belgrade in 1961 that wished to join neither the Western nor the Eastern alliance in the Cold War. Its leading figures were Nehru, Nasser, Tito and Sukarno; its forerunner was the Bandung Conference of 1955. The movement called for disarmament, an end to colonialism and a fairer world economy, and today comprises around 120 states.

A term for the rapid German campaigns of 1939 to 1941, in which armored formations and aircraft together thrust deep into the enemy's rear and caused the fronts to collapse within weeks. Poland, France and the Balkans were overrun in this way. Against the Soviet Union the concept failed, and the war became a long war of attrition in which the economic strength of the Allies proved decisive.

The epoch in which bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, was the most important material for weapons and tools; in the Near East roughly 3300 to 1200 BC, in central Europe 2200 to 800 BC. Because tin was rare, bronze promoted long-distance trade and the emergence of empires.

The movement of African Americans and their supporters which in the 1950s and 1960s fought racial segregation and exclusion from the vote in the southern states of the USA through nonviolent protest, boycotts and court cases. Its high points were the Montgomery bus boycott, the March on Washington in 1963 and the civil rights acts of 1964 and 1965. It became a model for freedom movements all over the world.

A branch of Protestantism going back to the Geneva reformer John Calvin. It emphasizes the predestination of human beings by God, a strict conduct of life and a church order carried by the congregations; the Huguenots, the Puritans and the Reformed churches of the Netherlands and Scotland belong to it.

A Chinese teaching based on the Tao Te Ching which calls on people to live in harmony with the Dao, the natural course of things. Instead of ambition and rigid rules it recommends serenity, simplicity and non-interference. Later a religion with temples, priests and doctrines of immortality developed out of it.

The dissolution of the European colonial empires after the Second World War, through which more than 80 states in Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific became independent between 1945 and 1975. It proceeded partly peacefully through negotiation, partly in long wars such as those in Indochina and Algeria. Economic dependence and colonial borders continued to have effects in many of the new states.

A central concept of the Indian religions which, depending on the context, denotes the cosmic order, religious duty or the teaching of the Buddha. For Hindus dharma means the duties of the individual according to his station and stage of life, for Buddhists the truth proclaimed by the Buddha. Ashoka understood by it a policy of nonviolence and welfare.

Protected non-Muslims, above all Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, who under Islamic rule were allowed to keep their religion and to administer their own communities. In return they paid a special poll tax and were subject to restrictions, for example on building new places of worship, on bearing arms and on access to high office. This arrangement was more tolerant than the treatment of religious minorities in the Europe of the time, but it did not mean equality of rights.

The false claim that the German army had remained undefeated in the field in the First World War and had only been stabbed in the back by strikes, revolution and the politicians at home. In fact the Supreme Army Command had itself demanded the armistice in the autumn of 1918. Nationalists and National Socialists used the legend to denigrate the Weimar Republic and its founders as traitors.

The transformation of wild plants and animals into crops and domestic animals through deliberate selection and breeding over many generations. The dog was domesticated as early as the Old Stone Age, grain, sheep, goat and cattle in the Neolithic, and the horse only in the Copper Age.

The form of rule in late antiquity from Diocletian onward, in which the emperor appeared openly as dominus, as lord, and was set apart from his subjects by diadem, purple, court ceremonial and divine veneration. Administration and army were tightly centralized; under the Christian emperors rule by the grace of God took the place of divinity.

In pre-revolutionary France, all those who belonged neither to the clergy nor to the nobility, that is, around 98 percent of the population, from wealthy merchants to day laborers. The Third Estate bore almost the entire tax burden but had only one of three votes in the Estates General. In 1789 its representatives declared themselves the National Assembly and thereby set off the Revolution.

A term for the sealed border between the Western democracies and the Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc, which divided Europe from the Baltic to the Adriatic. Winston Churchill made the term famous in a speech in 1946. Barbed wire, mines and orders to shoot prevented escape to the West; in 1989 the curtain was opened.

A long period of cold in which glaciers covered large parts of northern Europe, North America and the mountain ranges, and the sea level fell by more than 100 meters. The last Ice Age reached its peak around 20,000 years ago and ended about 12,000 years ago; over land bridges left dry, people reached America, among other places.

The policy of the 1970s of reducing tensions between East and West through negotiations, treaties and trade, without giving up the underlying opposition. It included Willy Brandt's Eastern Treaties, the agreements on the limitation of strategic arms and the Helsinki Final Act of 1975. It eased everyday life in divided Germany and prepared the way for the peaceful end of the Cold War.

The Law to Remedy the Distress of People and Reich, passed by the Reichstag on March 23, 1933, which allowed Hitler's government to issue laws without parliament and even in departure from the constitution. Only the SPD voted against it; the KPD deputies had already been arrested. The law was the legal basis of the dictatorship and was repeatedly extended until 1945.

The doctrine established by Charles Darwin in 1859 that the species of living things have developed from common ancestors over long periods of time. The driving force is natural selection: individuals with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more often. The theory is the foundation of modern biology.

The organization of production in large buildings in which many workers operate machines driven by a shared source of power, under supervision and to fixed hours. It replaced cottage industry and the crafts and created the class of wage laborers. Factory rules, the time clock and piece wages shaped working life from then on.

A political movement and form of rule founded in Italy by Benito Mussolini in 1919, combining extreme nationalism, the glorification of violence and leadership, the rejection of democracy and Marxism, and the bringing into line of state and society. After the March on Rome in 1922 Mussolini established the first fascist dictatorship, which became a model for similar movements in Europe. In a broader sense the term also denotes National Socialism and Franco's regime in Spain.

An almond-shaped stone tool worked on both sides, with sharp edges and a point, made from about 1.7 million years ago above all by Homo erectus. Hand axes served for cutting, scraping, chopping and digging and remained in use for over a million years.

The efforts of the Catholic Church from the middle of the 16th century onward to win back lost territories and to renew its own doctrine. The Council of Trent, the Jesuit order, the Inquisition and the banning of books, as well as the support of Catholic princes, were its most important means.

A model of political philosophy according to which the state rests on an agreement among free people and not on divine institution. Hobbes derived from it the necessity of a strong ruler, Locke the right of resistance, Rousseau the sovereignty of the people.

The principle of distributing state power among legislation, government and the administration of justice, so that no institution becomes too powerful. John Locke and above all Montesquieu developed the principle from the English constitution; today it is part of almost all democratic constitutions.

A fighter, usually a slave, prisoner of war or convict, who faced other gladiators or animals in arenas before an audience. Gladiators were trained in schools, fought with fixed categories of weapons and could win fame, money and freedom if successful. The games served politicians and emperors as a means of winning over the people.

The National Socialists' term for the subjection of all areas of state and society to the party in the years 1933 and 1934. State parliaments, trade unions, associations, the press, radio, culture and scholarship were dissolved, banned or filled with National Socialist leaders. Anyone who did not comply lost their position or was sent to a concentration camp.

The worldwide interconnection of economy, politics, culture and communication, which has accelerated sharply since the 1990s through free trade, container shipping, the internet and the rise of China. It lowered prices and poverty in many countries, but also led to the loss of industrial jobs in the West and made crises such as the financial crisis of 2008 and the coronavirus pandemic into worldwide events. Critics call for fairer rules of trade and more protection of the climate.

The architectural style of the High and Late Middle Ages, which arose in France around 1140 and combined the pointed arch, the ribbed vault and the buttress into tall churches flooded with light. Cathedrals such as Chartres, Reims and Cologne Cathedral are its most famous works; the name was coined only in the Renaissance, and as a term of disparagement.

An association of Low German merchants and later of cities which dominated trade in the North and Baltic Seas from the 12th to the 17th century. With trading posts in London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod, with joint diets and, if need be, with war, it enforced its trading privileges.

The epoch from Alexander's death in 323 BC to the Roman conquest of Egypt in 30 BC, in which the Greek language and Greek culture spread across the entire Near East and merged with oriental traditions. Its centers were Alexandria, Antioch and Pergamon; scholarship, art and trade flourished.

The pictorial writing of ancient Egypt, used from about 3200 BC on temple walls, tombs and papyrus. The signs stand for sounds, syllables or whole words. In 1822 Jean-François Champollion achieved their decipherment with the help of the Rosetta Stone.

The systematic, state-organized genocide of around six million European Jews by National Socialist Germany and its helpers between 1941 and 1945. It began with mass shootings behind the Eastern Front and was continued on an industrial scale with gas chambers in extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka and Sobibor. In Hebrew the crime is called the Shoah, catastrophe.

A printing process in which a whole page is cut in mirror image into a wooden block, inked and pressed onto paper. It arose in China in the Tang period and made possible the mass distribution of sutras, calendars and classics; the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated example.

The branch of the great apes which, after the separation from the chimpanzees around six to seven million years ago, led to human beings. It includes the australopithecines such as Lucy as well as all species of the genus Homo, of which only Homo sapiens is alive today.

A heavily armed Greek foot soldier with a round shield, spear, helmet and body armor, who paid for his own equipment. Hoplites fought shoulder to shoulder in the phalanx, a densely closed line of battle. Because the citizens defended the city as hoplites, they also demanded a political say.

The name for the French Protestants who followed the teaching of Calvin. After wars of religion they received freedom of belief in 1598 through the Edict of Nantes, which Louis XIV revoked in 1685; hundreds of thousands thereupon fled to Protestant countries, where they enriched crafts and the economy.

An educational movement of the 14th to 16th centuries which took its bearings from the writings of Greek and Roman antiquity and placed the human being, with reason and dignity, at the center. Humanists such as Erasmus searched for the original texts, criticized the church and promoted languages, history and rhetoric as the foundation of education.

Extreme devaluation of money, in which prices multiply within days or hours and money loses its function. In Germany, war debts, reparations and the financing of the struggle in the Ruhr by means of the printing press led in 1923 to a dollar costing 4.2 trillion marks. The destruction of the middle class's savings shook confidence in the republic for a long time to come.

The striving of great powers to extend their rule over other countries and peoples, whether through colonies, economic dependence or military pressure. The age of imperialism from about 1880 to 1914 brought almost all of Africa and large parts of Asia under European control and sharpened the rivalry of the powers.

The far-reaching change from an agrarian to an industrial society, which began in England around 1780. The steam engine, machines and factories replaced handwork and the workshop, and coal and iron became the most important raw materials. From about 1870 one speaks of a second Industrial Revolution, with electricity, chemistry and the internal combustion engine.

A conflict between the papacy and the monarchy in the 11th and 12th centuries over the question of who was entitled to install bishops and abbots in their office. Its best-known moment was Henry IV's journey to Canossa in 1077; the Concordat of Worms of 1122 separated spiritual from secular investiture.

Members of the most influential political club of the French Revolution, named after their meeting place in a former Dominican convent in Paris. Under Robespierre they became the radical party which from 1793 to 1794 defended the republic with terror against enemies at home and abroad. In Europe the term was long used as a term of abuse for supporters of radical democratic ideas.

The period from about 9500 BC in which people practiced farming and animal husbandry and lived in permanent villages. It is characterized by polished stone tools, pottery, weaving and large structures such as stone circles. It ended at different times in different regions with the beginning of metalworking.

The rule of the caliph, the successor of the Prophet Muhammad as head of the Muslim community. The first four caliphs were elected; thereafter the Umayyads and Abbasids made the office hereditary. From the 10th century onward several caliphates existed side by side and actual power passed to sultans; the Abbasid caliphate ended in 1258 with the destruction of Baghdad.

The conflict between the USA and the Soviet Union and their respective alliances from about 1947 to 1991. Both sides fought each other with an arms race, propaganda, espionage and proxy wars, but because of nuclear weapons never waged war directly against one another. It ended with the collapse of the Eastern Bloc and the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

The oldest known writing, developed by the Sumerians around 3200 BC. The signs were pressed into moist clay in wedge shapes with a reed stylus and at first denoted things, later also syllables. Cuneiform was used for over 3,000 years for many languages of the Near East.

The wars from 1792 to 1815 in which changing alliances of European powers, above all Great Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia, fought against revolutionary and Napoleonic France. They introduced mass armies of conscripts, changed the map of Europe and cost several million lives. The final phases are known in Germany as the Wars of Liberation.

A term for the exchange of plants, animals, diseases and people between the Old and the New World after 1492. The potato, maize and the tomato came to Europe, horses, cattle and wheat to America; smallpox and measles killed the greater part of the indigenous population.

Spanish conquerors who subjugated large parts of America with small forces in the 16th century. Men such as Hernán Cortés and Francisco Pizarro used firearms, horses, alliances with native peoples and imported epidemics to destroy the empires of the Aztecs and the Inca and to take possession of them for the Spanish Crown.

Camps in which from 1933 onward the National Socialists imprisoned, exploited and murdered political opponents and later Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses and people from the occupied countries without any court judgment. The SS operated a network of main camps such as Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen with over a thousand satellite camps. Historians distinguish the concentration camps, in which prisoners died through labor, hunger, disease and violence, from the pure extermination camps such as Treblinka, whose sole purpose was mass murder.

The holy scripture of Islam, which according to Muslim belief contains the revelations that Muhammad received from God between 610 and 632. The text was collected in an authoritative version around 650 under the third caliph Uthman and consists of 114 chapters, the suras. The Quran is the foundation of the faith, law and daily life of Muslims and shaped the Arabic language and calligraphy.

A military expedition proclaimed by the pope which promised its participants the forgiveness of sins and was directed above all against the Muslim rulers of the Holy Land. Between 1096 and 1291 seven great crusader armies marched east; later, campaigns against heretics and heathens in Europe were also given this name.

The transitional period between the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, in which people smelted copper ore and worked it into axes, needles and jewelry, while stone nevertheless remained the most important material. In Europe it covers roughly the time from 4500 to 2200 BC; Ötzi lived in this epoch.

A Chinese doctrine of the state from the Warring States period which relied not on morality and example, as Confucianism did, but on strict laws, harsh punishments and rewards. The state of Qin made it the basis of its rule and thereby unified China, but its severity contributed to the rapid fall of the Qin dynasty.

The largest unit of the Roman army, with about 4,000 to 6,000 heavily armed foot soldiers, divided into cohorts and centuries and supplemented by cavalry and auxiliary troops. From Marius onward legionaries served as professional soldiers for 16 to 25 years and afterward received land or money, which bound them to their commanders. In the imperial period around 30 legions stood on the frontiers.

The order of medieval Europe in which a lord granted a vassal land or an office as a fief, and the vassal in return owed him loyalty, counsel and military service. From the king through dukes and counts down to the simple knight, a chain of dependencies thus arose which took the place of the state.

A political current which places the freedom of the individual against the state at its center and calls for a constitution, the separation of powers, basic rights, a free press and a free economy. Liberalism arose out of the Enlightenment and the revolutions in America and France and was carried by the middle class. In the 19th century liberals contended with the forces of Restoration over constitutions and with democrats over the extension of the franchise.

The fortified frontier of the Roman Empire, consisting of ramparts, palisades, ditches, watchtowers and forts. The Upper German-Raetian Limes between the Rhine and the Danube was around 550 kilometers long, Hadrian's Wall in Britain 118 kilometers. The limes served less as an insurmountable wall than as a line of control for trade, customs and border traffic.

An Islamic institution of higher learning at which above all law, Quranic exegesis, the study of hadith and Arabic grammar were taught, often also mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Madrasas were usually financed by rulers or wealthy private individuals as a pious endowment and offered students lodging and food. Famous examples are al-Azhar in Cairo, al-Qarawiyyin in Fez and the schools of Timbuktu.

A Chinese conception according to which a ruler receives his power from Heaven for as long as he governs justly. Crop failures, catastrophes and uprisings were regarded as signs that the mandate had been withdrawn, and they justified the overthrow of a dynasty. The idea explains the cycle of the rise and fall of the Chinese dynasties.

A large, mostly unworked block of stone used in the Neolithic and Bronze Age for graves, stone rows and stone circles. Megalithic structures such as Stonehenge, Carnac and Newgrange are found above all along the Atlantic coast of Europe and show the organizational capacity of early farming societies.

The economic policy of absolutism, which measured the wealth of a state by its stock of gold and silver. The state promoted manufactories and exports, levied protective tariffs on imports and used colonies as sources of raw materials and as markets; Colbert under Louis XIV was its best-known representative.

A great Muslim empire in India, founded in 1526 by Babur, which under Akbar ruled the greater part of the subcontinent. It combined Persian, Central Asian and Indian culture, produced buildings such as the Taj Mahal, and fell apart in the 18th century before the British took over rule.

A way of life of men and women who commit themselves in monasteries, under a rule, to prayer, work and the renunciation of property, marriage and their own will. The Rule of Benedict of Nursia made the monasteries of the West into centers of learning, agriculture and the care of the sick.

The preservation of a corpse, in Egypt by removing the internal organs, drying with natron salt over 70 days and wrapping in linen bandages. The Egyptians believed that the body had to be preserved for continued life in the hereafter; the mummies of Ramesses II and Tutankhamun survive to this day.

The idea that people with a common language, culture and history form a nation which should have a state of its own. The French Revolution made the nation the bearer of sovereignty, and resistance against Napoleon awakened national feeling in Germany, Spain and Italy. In the 19th century nationalism was usually bound up with demands for freedom, but it later also developed into arrogance and hostility toward other peoples.

A state whose population understands itself as one nation with a common language, history and culture, and in which the state's borders are meant to coincide with that nation. In the 19th century it became the guiding political ideal and led to the unification of Italy and Germany, but also to the disintegration of the multiethnic empires.

A procedure of Athenian democracy in which once a year the citizens could scratch on potsherds the name of a politician whom they considered dangerous. Whoever received the most votes, provided at least 6,000 sherds had been cast, had to leave Athens for ten years, but kept his property and his citizenship. The aim was to prevent a new tyranny.

The title of the kings of ancient Egypt, derived from the Egyptian word for Great House, the palace. The pharaoh was regarded as the son of the sun god and the guarantor of Maat, the order of the world; he was at the same time chief priest, judge and commander of the army. More than 30 dynasties of pharaohs ruled Egypt for almost three millennia.

The Greek city-state, consisting of a city with its surrounding land and the community of its citizens, who governed themselves. There were hundreds of poleis, from Athens and Sparta to small island towns; their independence and rivalry shaped Greek history. The word politics derives from polis.

The form of rule established by Augustus in 27 BC, in which the emperor appeared as princeps, the first among equals, and formally left the republican institutions such as the Senate and the consuls in place. In fact power over the army, the provinces and the finances lay with the emperor. The Principate lasted until the crisis of the 3rd century.

The reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula by the Christian kingdoms of Asturias, León, Castile, Aragón and Portugal, which lasted from the 8th century to the fall of Granada in 1492. It did not proceed as an uninterrupted war, but with long phases of alliances, trade and cultural exchange across the frontier. After 1492 Jews and Muslims were expelled or forced to be baptized, which put an end to the religious diversity of Spain.

A movement of religious renewal which began in 1517 with Luther's 95 Theses and led to the division of Western Christendom into Catholics and Protestants. Its adherents appealed to scripture and faith alone, rejected indulgences and papal authority, and created churches of their own in Germany, Switzerland, Scandinavia, England and the Netherlands.

Payments and deliveries in kind which the loser of a war must render to the victors as compensation for war damage. The Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations on Germany which were fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks and included coal, locomotives and ships. The dispute over the payments led to the occupation of the Ruhr and was temporarily eased by the Dawes Plan of 1924 and the Young Plan of 1929, until the payments effectively ended in 1932.

The policy after 1815 which, proceeding from the Congress of Vienna, sought to restore the rule of the old dynasties and to push back the ideas of the Revolution. Its means were censorship, police surveillance, the banning of political associations and interventions against uprisings in Spain, Italy and Germany. Its most important representative was the Austrian state chancellor Metternich.

The adoption of the Roman language, way of life, legal order and style of town building by the population of the conquered provinces. It happened not through compulsion but through the settlement of veterans, trade, citizenship for the local elites and the attraction of baths, theaters and roads. Out of the Latin of the provinces the Romance languages emerged.

The Japanese term for the closing of the country under the Tokugawa shogunate from 1639 to 1854. Foreigners were not allowed to enter, Japanese were not allowed to leave the country, and foreign trade remained restricted to Chinese and Dutch merchants at Nagasaki; the country experienced two centuries of peace without European influence.

A province of the Persian Empire, administered by a governor, the satrap, in the name of the Great King. The satraps collected taxes, provided troops and administered justice, but were supervised by royal inspectors. The system allowed the Achaemenids to hold together an empire of many peoples and languages.

The scholarly method of the medieval universities, which examined questions of faith with the means of logic and the philosophy of Aristotle. Theses were tested in regulated disputations and objections refuted; Thomas Aquinas brought scholasticism to its high point in the 13th century.

A network of caravan routes and sea routes which from the Han period onward connected China by way of Central Asia and Persia with India and the Mediterranean world. Alongside silk, spices, glass and horses, religions such as Buddhism, techniques such as papermaking, and diseases also traveled along it. The name dates only from the 19th century.

The council of Rome's former officeholders, originally of the elders, with about 300 to 600 members appointed for life. In the Republic the Senate determined foreign policy, finances and provincial administration and was the center of the nobility's power. In the imperial period it lost influence, but survived as an honorary assembly into late antiquity.

The term for the distress of the working class in the 19th century: low wages, long working hours, child labor, wretched housing and the absence of provision for sickness and old age. Churches, entrepreneurs, socialists and the state sought different answers, from company housing through trade unions to social insurance.

Compulsory insurance organized by the state which protects employees against sickness, accident, old age and disability and is financed by contributions from employers and employees. It was introduced by Bismarck in the German Empire between 1883 and 1889 and became a model for welfare states all over the world.

An independent state consisting of a city and its surrounding land. In Sumer each city-state was dedicated to a god of its own and was ruled by a king or priestly prince; the cities fought one another over water and land until Sargon of Akkad united them into a single empire.

The division of medieval society into estates by birth, with different rights and duties: the clergy, the nobility and the great remainder of peasants and townspeople. According to the doctrine of the time, the first prayed, the second fought and the third worked; uprisings such as that of 1381 in England called this order into question.

A way of waging war in which opposing armies face each other in fortified trenches and the front scarcely moves for months or years. On the Western Front of the First World War, machine guns, artillery and barbed wire made every attack so costly that both sides remained in their trenches until 1918. Verdun and the Somme are the best-known examples.

A war in which great powers do not fight each other themselves but support hostile parties in a third country with weapons, money, advisers or troops of their own. In the Cold War the USA and the Soviet Union carried out their opposition in this way in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and Africa. Those who suffered were above all the populations of these countries.

The mystical current of Islam, which strives for an immediate, loving experience of God and uses prayer, meditation, song, dance and asceticism to that end. Sufis such as Rabia of Basra, al-Ghazali and Rumi created important poetry and philosophy; from the 12th century onward they joined together in orders with masters and disciples. Sufi brotherhoods carried Islam to Anatolia, India, Southeast Asia and Africa.

The two great currents of Islam, which arose out of the dispute over the succession to Muhammad. The Shiites regard Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants as the only legitimate leaders; the Sunnis recognize the elected caliphs and appeal to the Sunna, the example of the Prophet. Around 85 to 90 percent of Muslims today are Sunnis; Shiites live above all in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon and Bahrain.

A war in which a state mobilizes all its people, economic forces and resources for the struggle and the line between soldiers and civilians becomes blurred. The First World War is regarded as the first total war: factories produced only for the front, women replaced men at work, and blockades left the civilian population to go hungry. Propaganda and censorship were meant to secure the will to hold out.

A serious drama which arose in Athens in the 5th century BC out of the choral songs in honor of Dionysus. The tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides show heroes from myth and history in conflict with the gods, the law and fate, and were performed at competitions before thousands of citizens.

The sole rule of a man who seized power without any legal basis, usually by force or with the support of the people against the nobility. In the 7th and 6th centuries BC tyrants ruled in many Greek cities and often promoted the economy and the arts; only later did the term become an expression for violent despotism.

The term for the German war against the Soviet Union from 1941, which from the outset aimed not merely at military victory but at the destruction of the state, the murder of the Jews and of communist officials, and the death by starvation of millions of civilians and prisoners of war. Orders such as the Commissar Order suspended the law of war. The Wehrmacht was directly involved in this.

A territory which after the First World War was detached from the possessions of Germany or of the Ottoman Empire and administered by a victorious power on behalf of the League of Nations, supposedly until it was ready for independence. Great Britain received Palestine, Iraq and Transjordan, France Syria and Lebanon; the German colonies went to Great Britain, France, Belgium, Japan and others. In practice the mandates differed hardly at all from colonies.

The period from the invasion of the Huns around 375 to about 568, in which Germanic peoples such as the Goths, Vandals, Franks and Lombards pushed into the Roman Empire and founded kingdoms of their own there. It led to the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 and to the emergence of the medieval states of Europe; its causes were the search for land, population pressure and the pressure of the Huns.

The principle that all state power proceeds from the people and that rulers exercise their power only as agents of the people. It was formulated by Rousseau, anchored in 1776 in the American Declaration of Independence and in 1789 in the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, and replaced the divine right of kings. Popular sovereignty is to this day the foundation of democratic constitutions.

The period in Germany between the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and the March Revolution of 1848, in which liberal and national movements grew despite censorship and persecution. Student fraternities, the Hambach Festival, writers such as Heine and Büchner, and uprisings such as that of the Silesian weavers marked these years. The term looks back from the Revolution of 1848 to the time before it.

The name for the German state from 1918 to 1933, after the city of Weimar, where the National Assembly adopted the constitution in 1919. The first German democracy stood from the beginning under the pressure of the Treaty of Versailles, inflation, attempted coups and political violence. After a brief stabilization in the Golden Twenties it broke apart under the Great Depression and ended with Hitler's appointment as Reich Chancellor.

The rapid division of almost the entire African continent among the European colonial powers between about 1880 and 1914. The Berlin Conference of 1884/85 laid down the rules of the game, without any Africans taking part. Borders were drawn on the drawing board and in many cases still exist today.

A collective term for all forms of opposition to the Nazi regime, from the refusal to give the Hitler salute through leaflets and the hiding of the persecuted to assassination attempts and plans for a coup. It was carried by communists and social democrats, Christians, students, officers and individuals acting alone such as Georg Elser, but it always remained a small minority. In the occupied countries partisans and underground movements such as the Résistance fought against German rule.

A stepped temple tower of mud brick in Mesopotamia, on whose summit stood a sanctuary of the city god. The ziggurat of Ur, from around 2100 BC, is the best preserved; the biblical Tower of Babel goes back to the ziggurat of Babylon.
